The commercial reagents used in this study were as follows: Bafilomycin A1 (Baf; Selleck, S1413), KN-93 phosphate (Selleck, S7423), LysoTracker (Invitrogen, L7528), and LysoSensor Yellow/Blue probe (Invitrogen, L7545).

Cell culture and transfection
HEK293T cells (ATCC, CRL-3216), HeLa cells (ATCC, CCL-2), Vero cells (ATCC, CCL-81), and RAW264.7 cells (ATCC, TIB-71) were obtained from the American type culture collection (ATCC). The above cell lines were all cultured in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM; Invitrogen, C11995500BT) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, 16000-044) at 37ºC in a humidified 5% CO2 incubator. In related experiments, the transfection of HEK293T or HeLa cells was carried out with KunGre™ Liposomal Transfection Reagent (Greact, GT201-03) according to the manufacturers’ instructions.

Recombinant protein expression and purification
For prokaryotic expression of GST, GST-Rab14, GST-RUFY1, and His-CAMK2D, E. coli BL21 (DE3) strains harboring GST or His derivatives were grown in LB medium supplemented with the indicated antibiotics at 37°C until the OD600 = 0.6. Then, 0.1 mM Isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) was added to the cultures to induce the expression of proteins at 16°C for 16 hours. Bacteria were then harvested by centrifugation at 6,500 ×g for 10 minutes and suspended in a buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 150 mM NaCl. Subsequently, cells were broken using Low-temperature Ultra-high Pressure Continuous Flow Cell Disrupters (JNBIO) for collecting the supernatants. Glutathione Sepharose 4B (GE Healthcare, 17-0756-05) and Ni-NTA Agarose (Qiagen, 30230) were added to the supernatants for purification of GST- or His-tagged proteins, respectively. For eukaryotic expression and purification of GFP-tagged V0a1 or its mutants, Hela cells were transfected with the indicated plasmids for 24 hours and were then lysed in the RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime Biotechnology, P0013D) supplemented with 1% protease inhibitor cocktail (Bimake, B14001) at 4°C for 10 minutes. The cell lysates were then incubated with anti-GFP-Nanoab-Agarose (LABLEAD, GNA-50-1000) at 4°C for 4 hours. After extensively washing with the lysis buffer, the GFP-tagged proteins were eluted by 50 μL elution buffer (0.2 mM glycine, adjust pH to 2.5 by HCl) and neutralized by 5 μL neutralization buffer (1.0 M Tris-HCl, pH 10.4). Protein concentrations were determined by the BCA protein assay (Beyotime, P0009) and protein purity was examined by SDS-PAGE analysis.

Establishment of knockout and knockdown cell lines
RAW264.7 cells and Hela cells with Rab14 or CAMK2D knocking out were generated using the CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing system. Specifically, the sgRNA sequences targeting Rab14 or CAMK2D (see Supplementary Data 3) were predicted by the CRISPR-Gold (https://crisprgold.mdc-berlin.de/) and were then cloned into the pSpCas9(BB)-2A-GFP vector (Addgene, 48138). Next, RAW264.7 cells and Hela cells were transfected with the specific recombinant plasmid for 24 hours. The single cell with green fluorescence was sorted with BD FACSAria III cell sorter (BD Biosciences) and was then identified by immunoblotting analysis with the antibody against Rab14 or CAMK2D.

For knocking down Rab genes in RAW264.7 cells, the siRNA sequences targeting the specific Rab (see Supplementary Data 3) were designed by BLOCK-iT™ RNAi Designer. Then, 40 pM siRNAs targeting each Rab gene were transfected into RAW264.7 cells by using KunGreTM Liposomal Transfection Reagent (Greact, GT201-03) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. After 12 hours, cells were re-transfected with the sgRNAs and were then further incubated for another 12 hours. The knocking down efficiency of Rab genes was verified by the quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) analysis. V0a1-knocking down Rab14+/+ and Rab14-/- RAW264.7 cells were generated in the same as above and were then identified by immunoblotting analysis with the antibody against V0a1.

qPCR analysis
RAW264.7 cells transfected with Rab siRNAs were collected for total RNA extraction using the Total RNA Extraction Kit (Dongsheng, R1061). Then, the RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the Hifair First Strand cDNA Synthesis SuperMix (YEASEN, 11141ES60). The cDNA was then analyzed by qPCR using Hieff qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix (YEASEN, 11202ES08) on an ABI 7500 system (Applied Biosystems). Quantitative expression of the targeted genes was normalized to Gapdh and analyzed by the 2−ΔΔCT method. All qPCR primers are listed in Supplementary Data 3.

Establishment of RAW264.7 cells stably expressing mCherry-GFP-LC3
RAW264.7 cells stably expressing mCherry-GFP-LC3 were generated as described previously49. Briefly, PMSCV puro-mCherry-GFP-LC3 and the two packaging plasmids including pVSV-G and pCMV-Gag-Pol were co-transfected to HEK293T cells for obtaining lentivirus. Then, the lentiviral supernatant was collected at 48 hours post-transfection, filtered with a 0.45-μm filter, and concentrated by Lentivirus Concentration Solution (YEASEN, 41101ES50). The medium containing lentivirus was used to infect RAW264.7 cells, and the cells stably expressing mCherry-GFP-LC3 were selected using 2 μg/mL puromycin (Selleck, s7417). The expression of mCherry-GFP-LC3 was verified by immunofluorescence microscopy.

Measurement of phagolysosomal pH
The pH of pathogen-containing phagolysosomes was detected as described previously59. Briefly, the model pathogen M. smegmatis was first labeled with 20 μM pHrodo Red succinimidyl ester (Invitrogen, P36600) at 37°C for 1 hour. Next, the labelled bacteria were washed three times with Middlebrook 7H9 media containing 0.05% Tween-80 and were then labeled with 25 μg/mL Alexa Fluor 488 succinimidyl ester (Invitrogen, A20000) at 37°C for 1 hour. After washing again, bacterial pellets were resuspended in DMEM containing 0.05% Tween-80. Thereafter, RAW264.7 cells were infected with the double-labeled M. smegmatis at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 10 for 2 hours and were then washed with 1 × PBS to remove any non-internalized bacteria. The infection was incubated for another 2 hours at 37°C with 5% CO2, and the fluorescence intensity in the RAW264.7 cells was analyzed by Flow cytometer (BD LSRFortessa SORP) and FlowJo (v10) software. The phagolysosomal pH was calculated by the mean fluorescence ratios of pHrodo and Alexa Fluor 488.

Pathogen infections of macrophages
RAW264.7 cells were seeded at 1 × 106 cells per well in 6-well plates and cultured at 37ºC with 5% CO2 overnight. For M. smegmatis infection, frozen bacteria that have grown to mid-logarithmic phase were thawed and were then centrifuged and resuspended in DMEM medium with 0.05% Tween-80 to infect RAW264.7 cells at a MOI of 10. After 2 hours of infection, cells were washed three times with 1 × PBS to exclude non-internalized bacteria and were then incubated with the fresh DMEM medium supplemented with 10 μg/mL gentamicin to kill non-washed extracellular bacteria. At the indicated time points, cells were harvested for colony-forming unit (CFU) counting analysis, immunoblotting analysis, and immunofluorescence analysis. For L. monocytogenes infection, bacteria were grown in BHI broth to mid-log phase and were then resuspended in DMEM medium to infect RAW264.7 cells at a MOI of 5. After 1 hour of infection, cells were washed with 1 × PBS to exclude non-internalized bacteria and were then incubated with the fresh DMEM medium supplemented with 10 μg/mL gentamicin until the indicated time points for further CFU, immunoblotting, and immunofluorescence analysis. For viral infection, the DNA virus HSV-1 and RNA virus SeV were both used to infect RAW264.7 cells at a MOI of 1. At the indicated time points, the cells were collected for virus copy number, immunoblotting, and immunofluorescence analysis. For inhibition of CAMK2D or autophagy flux, cells were treated with 10 μM KN-93-P or 50 nM Baf, respectively, and the control groups were treated with equal volume of dimethyl sulfoxide.

CTSD activity assay
CTSD activity was measured using a commercial assay kit (Abcam, ab65302). Briefly, harvested cells were lysed in chilled buffer, and the lysates were incubated with the substrate-containing reaction mix at 37°C for 1–2 hours, protected from light. Fluorescence was measured at Ex/Em = 328/460 nm using a microplate reader. Enzyme activity was determined based on the fold change in relative fluorescence units (RFU) of treated samples compared to control samples.

CFU counting analysis of bacteria and plaque assay of virus
For CFU counting analysis of M. smegmatis or L. monocytogenes, infected macrophages or tissues were lysed in 1 × PBS containing 0.05% SDS. Then, the cell lysates were plated by serial dilution on 7H10 agar plates for 72 hours or on BHI agar plates for 24 hours, respectively. For plaque assay of virus, the homogenates of lungs or spleens were harvested and diluted to infect confluent Vero cells. At 2 hours post infection, the supernatant was removed and the infected Vero cells were overlaied with a mixed medium of 2% low melting point agarose (YEASEN, 10214ES08) and 2% FBS at a ratio of 1:1. After 72 hours post infection, the overlay was removed and the cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich, 441244) for 15 minutes and stained with 0.1% crystal violetin (Huaaobio, 01-174) for 30 minutes. Then, the plaques were counted, averaged, and multiplied by the dilution factor to determine viral titers as PFU/mL. Virus copy numbers were determined by qPCR using the corresponding primers (Supplementary Data 3).

ER and lysosome extraction
ER and lysosomal fractions were isolated using the Endoplasmic Reticulum Extraction Kit (Solarbio, EX1370) and the Lysosome Enrichment Kit (Thermo Scientific, 89839), respectively. Briefly, cells were homogenized using a Dounce homogenizer, followed by ER enrichment through differential centrifugation and lysosome purification via density gradient separation according to the manufacturers’ instructions. All procedures were performed at 4°C with pre-cooled reagents.

Immunoprecipitation
For immunoprecipitation of V0a1 or Rab14 from RAW264.7 cells, cells were lysed with the RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with 1% protease inhibitor cocktail at 4°C for 10 minutes. Then, cell lysates were incubated with the antibody against V0a1 or Rab14 and protein A/G agarose (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-2003) at 4°C, followed by washing with the RIPA lysis buffer for three times. For co-immunoprecipitation of two proteins co-overexpressed in HEK293T cells, cells were lysed in the RIPA lysis buffer at 4°C and were then incubated with anti-Flag M2 Affinity Gel (Sigma-Aldrich, A2220), anti-Myc Agarose (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-40AC), or anti-GFP-Nanoab-Agarose (LABLEAD, GNA-50-1000) at 4°C for 4 hours. Thereafter, the cells were washed with the RIPA lysis buffer for three times. The immunoprecipitated samples were analyzed by immunoblotting with the indicated antibodies.

In vitro precipitation assay
For competitive binding analysis, 5 μg of His-CAMK2D was incubated with 20 μL of Ni-NTA Agarose in 500 μL binding buffer (50 mM Tris, pH 7.5, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM DTT, and 0.1% NP-40) containing 1% protease inhibitor cocktail for 1 hour at 4°C. Then, the agaroses carrying His-CAMK2D were collected and washed three times with the binding buffer, followed by incubating with 13 μg of purified GFP-V0a1 in the presence or absence of 1μg, 2 μg of GST or 2 μg, 5 μg of GST-Rab14 in the binding buffer for 4 hours at 4°C. After three washes, the bound protein complexes were finally subjected to immunoblotting analysis.

Acyl-Rac assay
The acyl-Rac assay was conducted to determine the S-palmitoylation of proteins as described previously60, 61. Briefly, proteins from cell lysates were incubated with blocking buffer (100 mM HEPES, 1 mM EDTA, 2.5 % SDS, 50 mM N- ethylmaleimide, pH 7.5) at 50℃ for 1 hour, followed by precipitation with three volumes of ice-cold acetone at -20℃ for 20 minutes. After centrifugation at 5,000 ×g for 10 minutes, the pellet was washed four times with 70% acetone. Next, the pellet was resuspended in binding buffer (100 mM HEPES, 1.0 mM EDTA, 1 % SDS, pH 7.5) and split into two aliquots. One aliquot was treated with 2 M NH2OH (freshly prepared, pH 7.5) to specifically cleave thioester bonds and expose nascent thiol groups, while the other was treated with PBS as a negative control. The newly exposed thiols were then biotinylated using EZ-Link™ HPDP-Biotin (Thermo Scientific, A35390). Biotinylated proteins were affinity-purified with Pierce™ streptavidin coated magnetic beads (Thermo Scientific, 89891) at room temperature for 2 hours. After three washes, the beads were mixed with loading buffer and subjected to immunoblotting analysis.

Immunoblotting analysis
Proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE gels and transferred to the polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane (Millipore, IPVH00010). The membranes were blocked with 5% (w/v) nonfat dry milk in Tris-buffered saline containing 0.1% Tween-20 (TBST) solution for 1 hour at room temperature and were then incubated with specific primary antibodies overnight at 4°C. Thereafter, the membranes were washed with TBST for three times and were then incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature followed by three washes with TBST. Finally, the membranes were developed by Immobilon Western Chemiluminescent HRP Substrate (Millipore, WBKLS0500) and exposed to X-ray film. For quantifications, densitometry was performed using ImageJ (v1.8.0) to evaluate the intensity of the immunoblotting band signals. The uncropped and unprocessed scans of all blots are provided in the Source Data file.

Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis
For identifying Rab14-interacting proteins by MS analysis, immunoprecipitates of Flag or Flag-Rab14 were separated by SDS-PAGE. Then, the gels were stained with the Coomassie brilliant blue and the indicated bands were excised. Thereafter, the bands were rinsed with 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate, dried, and reduced using 10 mM dithiothreitol (DTT) in 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate at 56°C and were then alkylated with 55 mM iodoacetamide. Proteins were digested with 12.5 ng/μL trypsin overnight at room temperature, and the peptide mixture was extracted by 60% acetonitrile. Next, samples were desalted on a C18 ZipTip pipette tip (Millipore) and were separated via Nano LC-MS/MS analysis on a NanoAcquity system (Waters, Milford, MA) connected to an LTQ-Orbitrap XL hybrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany). The MS raw files were processed using Proteome Discoverer (Version 1.4.0.288, Thermo Fischer Scientific) and were then searched against the Uniprot_human_2018 database by using the SEQUEST engine. The differential proteins with at least five unique peptides in the Flag-Rab14 group compared with the Flag group were considered the potential interactive proteins of Rab14, and the protein-protein interaction network diagram of Rab14-interacting proteins was edited by utilizing Adobe Illustrator CS6 (AI) software.

Immunofluorescence microscopy
Cells were seeded on cover glasses in 6-well cell culture plates and were then transfected with the indicated plasmids or infected with the indicated pathogens. Specifically, for detecting the colocalization of proteins with subcellular organelles, GFP-V0a1, GFP-V0a2, GFP-V0a3, or GFP-LC3 was transfected to Hela cells for 24 hours. Then, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 10 minutes, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 (Solarbio, T8200) for 15 minutes, and blocked with 5% BSA (Solarbio, A8010) for 30 minutes at room temperature. Primary antibodies against subcellular organelles including ER (anti-calnexin), Golgi (anti-GM130), early endosomes (anti-Rab5), late endosomes (anti-Rab7), and lysosomes (anti-LAMP1) were incubated with the cells for 2 hours at room temperature. After washing three times with 1 × PBS, the fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies were applied for 1 hour. After washing again, slides were mounted with medium containing 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI, Beyotime, C1002). For detecting lysosomal acidification during pathogen infections, RAW264.7 cells were infected with the indicated pathogen as described above and were then incubated with 75 nM LysoTracker for an additional 30 minutes. Next, cells were fixed and stained with DAPI. For detecting autophagy flux during pathogen infections, RAW264.7 cells stably expressing mCherry-GFP-LC3 were infected with the indicated pathogen as described above and were then fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde. For microscopy analysis, confocal images were taken with the Leica SP8 confocal microscope (Leica Microsystems) and analyzed by the Leica Application Suite Las X (v2.0.1.14392) software. For the image quantifications, approximately 50 cells were analyzed with ImageJ (v1.8.0) for each biological replicate, and the data was shown as the mean ± SEM of three independent experiments.

Live-cell imaging
For detecting V0a1 subcellular localization, Rab14+/+ and Rab14-/- RAW264.7 cells were plated on Glass Bottom Culture Dishes (NEST, 801002) and were then transfected with GFP-V0a1 for 24 hours. Thereafter, cells were infected with M. smegmatis prestained with Alexa FlourTM405 (Invitrogen, A30000) at a MOI of 10 for 2 hours and were then incubated with 75 nM LysoTracker for 30 minutes. Next, imaging was performed using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope equipped with an environmental control chamber providing 37°C, 5% CO2, and 20–30% humidity. Images were acquired in 5 minutes intervals over a time frame of 4 hours. For examining lysosomal acidification, the LysoSensor Yellow/Blue probe was added at 2 μM to cells and incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes. After being washed twice with pre-warmed growth medium, the cells were immediately visualized using a Leica SP8 confocal microscope. The fluorescence intensities in the blue and yellow channels were quantified using ImageJ (v1.8.0).

Molecular docking and multiple sequence alignment analysis
Molecular docking analysis of V0a1 and CAMK2D was performed as described previously62. Briefly, the structure of V0a1 (AlphaFold DB: AF-Q93050-F1) was predicted using AlphaFold 3, and the solved crystal structure of CAMK2D (PDB: 5VLO) was obtained from the RCSB PDB database. Both structures were then prepared by removing water molecules, heteroatoms, and co-crystallized ligands, followed by the addition of polar hydrogen atoms. The protein–protein molecular docking of V0a1 and CAMK2D was performed by ClusPro web server (https://cluspro.org). Interface analysis was performed using the PISA web server (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pdbe/pisa/). Visualization and superimposition of docking poses and crystallographic structures were done using PyMOL (v.2.5.7). Additionally, multiple sequence alignment of V0a1, V0a2, and V0a3 was performed using ESPript 3.0 server (https://espript.ibcp.fr/ESPript/cgi-bin/ESPript.cgi). Conserved residues are marked with the red background.

In vitro and in vivo phosphorylation assay
In vitro phosphorylation assay detecting CAMK2D-mediated V0a1 phosphorylation was performed as described previously63. Briefly, 13 μg purified GFP-V0a1 or its mutants was incubated with 5 μg His-CAMK2D in the presence or absence of 5 μg GST-Rab14 in 200 μL kinase reaction buffer (10 mM HEPES, pH 7.2, 1 mM EGTA, 5 mM MgCl2, 2 mM CaCl2, and 0.4 mM ATP) supplemented with 1% protease inhibitor cocktail and 1% phosphatase inhibitor cocktail. After incubation at 30°C for 30 minutes, the reaction was terminated by the addition of SDS loading buffer and subjected to SDS-PAGE analysis. V0a2 and V0a3 phosphorylation was examined using the same method. For in vivo phosphorylation assay, V0a1 or its mutant was immunoprecipitated from Rab14+/+ and Rab14-/- cells and was then subjected to immunoblotting with the antibody against p-Ser or p-Thr.

Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0 software (https://www.graphpad.com/). All data were analyzed using unpaired two-sided Student’s t-test, one-way ANOVA, or two-way ANOVA analysis followed by multiple comparisons as indicated in the corresponding figure legends. Data are shown as mean and standard error of mean (s.e.m.). Unless otherwise indicated, at least two biological replicates were included in all experiments. Additional details about the statistical analysis of experiments and number of biological replicates (n) are indicated in the corresponding figure legends.

Data availability
All data are available in the main text and the supplementary materials. The plasmids and cell lines generated in this study are available from the corresponding author. Source data are provided with this paper.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The host-directed restriction factors against viral infections are well studied. However, such factors against bacterial
pathogens largely remain unexplored. Lei and colleagues in their manuscript (NCOMMS-25-55033-T) entitled “Rab14
restricts pathogens by promoting V-ATPase lysosomal delivery to drive lysosomal acidification” conducted a comprehensive
screening of host factors that promote lysosomal acidification, which is essential for pathogen clearance from infected cells.
They screened host factors that promote lysosomal acidification, and identified a small GTPase, Rab14, as a restriction
factor with broad-spectrum activity against multiple viruses and bacteria. Since
lysosomal acidification is essential for lysosomal acid hydrolases to degrade the
pathogens, they focused their investigations on understanding the mechanism
underlying the events that follow an infection. They found that upon infection by a pathogen, the level of GTP-bound Rab14
binding to Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase 2 (CAMK2D) increases. This process suppressed CAMK2D-
mediated phosphorylation of V0a1, a critical subunit essential for the assembly of the multi-protein complex representing
functional V-ATPase, which acidifies the lysosomal lumen. The results of their study have uncovered a previously
unrecognized intrinsic mechanism that regulates the innate immune response that protects an organism against infection by
bacterial pathogens.
General comments-
This is an imaginative, well-designed and executed study that provides a considerable amount of novel information that may
be useful for the development of effective therapeutics against antibiotic-resistant bacterial pathogens. Having said that,
some of the results of this study may require further elaboration to fully explain the proposed mechanisms. Therefore, the
manuscript may require some major revisions.
Specific comments:
1.
Previous mechanistic studies have shown that Rab14 stimulates organellar fusion (e.g. phagosomes-early endosome) but
not between phagosome and late endosome/lysosome. Moreover, Rab14 has been reported to enable phagosomes
containing tuberculosis bacteria to maintain early endosomal characteristics and thereby, resist the progression to late
endosomal / lysosomal degradative functon(https://doi:10.1038/sj.emboj.7601407). Since autophagosome-lysosome fusion
is critical for the catalytic function of the lysosomal acid hydrolases that are essential for degrading the contents of the
autophagosomes. The authors should also discuss how Rab14-CAMK2D-mediated phosphorylation of V0a1 may
coordinately regulate the two processes (i.e. the localization of V0a1 on lysosomal membrane to maintain lysosomal
acidification by VATPase and the autophagosome-lysosome fusion).
2.
The authors highlighted the critical roles of Rab14 in host-directed restriction against pathogens. However, recent reports
indicate that both Rab2 and Rab14 are important in autophagosome maturation and function requiring lysosomal
acidic environment (https://doi.org/10.1080/15548627.2024.2374699), which is maintained by active V-ATPase on
lysosomal membrane. The authors should discuss whether Rab2, in addition to Rab14, plays any role in lysosomal
acidification in their experimental system.
3.
On page 7/79, lines 152-156, the authors state that while V0a1 strongly colocalized with LAMP1-positive lysosomes in
Rab14+/+ cells, it primarily colocalized with the ER-marker, calnexin in Rab14-/- cells. The anterograde movement (from ER
to Golgi) of proteins is mediated by COPII vesicles. In addition, all COPII proteins, except Sec13, have been reported to
undergo S-palmitoylation (https://doi:10.1016/j.nbd.2025.106890), a reversable post-translational modification of proteins by
saturated fatty acids (generally palmitate). Moreover, dynamic S-palmitoylation (palmitoylation-depalmitoylation) has been
shown to facilitate the trafficking of V0a1 to the late endosome / lysosome (https://doi:10.1038/ncomms14612). Thus, both S-
palmitoylation and depalmitoylation, catalyzed by ZDHHC palmitoyl acyl transferases (PATs) and thioesterases,
respectively, are critical for V0a1 to successfully traffic to the late endosomal / lysosomal membrane
(https://doi:10.1098/rsob.200411). Indeed, it has been reported that the handover of V0a1 from the sorting endosome to late
endosome / lysosome requires dynamic S-palmitoylation. Therefore, it is critically important for the authors to rule out that in
Rab14-/- cells, the dynamic S-palmitoylation of V0a1 is not compromised impairing the assembly of VATPase multiprotein
complex essential for trafficking from the ER to the lysosomal membrane.
4.
The authors have demonstrated that in Rab14-/- cells V0a1 colocalizes with the ER marker, calnexin. This may suggest that
the ER-Golgi trafficking is also defective in these cells. Since COPII proteins (e.g. Sar1, Sec23/Sec24) except Sec 13 are
also reported to be S-palmitoylated (https://doi: 10.1016/j.nbd.2025.106890), and a thioesterase (PPT1)-deficiency impairs
anterograde (ER to Golgi) trafficking mediated by COPII vesicles, it is therefore critically important for the authors to
demonstrate that dynamic S-palmitoylation of COPII-associated proteins are not adversely affected in Rab14-/- cells.
5.
A role for Rab14 in stimulating the fusion of phagosomes with early endosomes but not with late endosomes has been
demonstrated in mechanistic studies (https://doi:10.1038/sj.emboj.7601407). In case of mycobacterial pathogens, it has
been shown that Rab14 enables phagosomes to maintain early endosomal characteristics but not those of late
endosomal/lysosomal degradative components. The authors should discuss this finding considering their proposed immune
mechanism mediated by Rab14-CAM2D-V-ATPase axis.

Specific comments:
1. Previous mechanistic studies have shown that Rab14 stimulates organellar fusion
(e.g. phagosomes-early endosome) but not between phagosome and late
endosome/lysosome. Moreover, Rab14 has been reported to enable phagosomes
containing tuberculosis bacteria to maintain early endosomal characteristics and

critical for the catalytic function of the lysosomal acid hydrolases that are essential for
degrading the contents of the autophagosomes. The authors should also discuss how

R: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point. As noted by the reviewer,
Rab14 has been reported to promote phagosome-early endosome fusion while
suppressing phagosome fusion with late endosomes or lysosomes (PMID:
17082769). However, it should be mentioned that this function was characterized
in macrophages infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), a chronic
pathogen that usually hijacks host factors to inhibit immune responses for its long-
term survival (PMID: 32728204). For example, Mtb can employ its effectors (such
as PknG) to suppress Rab14-GTP hydrolysis, leading to the constitutive activation
of Rab14, which arrests phagosomes at the early endosome stage and prevents
their fusion with late endosomes and lysosomes, thereby blocking phagosomal
maturation and pathogen clearance (PMID: 17082769; PMID: 34092182). In
contrast, in macrophages infected with heat-killed Mtb, Rab14 only transiently
associates with phagosomes, permitting their normal fusion with late endosomes
and lysosomes for bacterial clearance (PMID: 17082769). Thus, the previously
observed effect of Rab14 stimulating organellar fusion between phagosomes and
early endosomes, but not with late endosomes or lysosomes, may represent a
pathogen-hijacked state. In our study, instead of using Mtb that hijacks Rab14
function, we used model pathogens (including Mycobacterium smegmatis, Listeria
monocytogenes, DNA virus HSV-1, and RNA virus SeV) that can be rapidly cleared
by the host immune system to investigate the uncompromised, physiological
function of Rab14, and we demonstrate that Rab14 primarily facilitates pathogen
clearance by promoting V0a1 lysosomal localization and subsequent lysosomal
acidification through suppression of CAMK2D-mediated V0a1 phosphorylation.
Furthermore, we performed confocal microscopy experiments to address the
reviewer’s query regarding whether the Rab14-CAMK2D axis modulates the
autophagosome-lysosome fusion step, and we found that the Rab14-CAMK2D axis
did not regulate this process in macrophages (revised Supplementary Fig. 13; lines
375–384). Thus, Rab14-CAMK2D-mediated phosphorylation of V0a1 regulates
the localization of V0a1 on lysosomal membrane to maintain lysosomal
acidification by V-ATPase without affecting the autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
It should be noticed that our macrophage-based results are different from a
previous study reporting that Rab14 promotes autophagosome-lysosome fusion in
MDCK epithelial cells (PMID: 38953305), indicating that the function of Rab14 is
cell type-dependent, which is further supported in other studies. For instance,
Rab14 promotes the trafficking of glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) from early
endosomes to the Golgi apparatus following endocytosis in adipocytes (PMID:
23444368; PMID: 26936971), while facilitating the GLUT4 translocation from the
GLUT4 storage vesicles (GSV) compartment to the plasma membrane in muscle
cells (PMID: 18701652).
Taken together, Rab14 is a critical host restriction factor whose activity is fine-
tuned by cell-type-specific mechanisms, which process could also be exploited by
certain pathogens for their immune evasion. We have expanded our discussion
accordingly (lines 433–434, 440–451).
2. The authors highlighted the critical roles of Rab14 in host-directed restriction against
pathogens. However, recent reports indicate that both Rab2 and Rab14 are important in
autophagosome maturation and function requiring lysosomal acidic environment
(https://doi.org/10.1080/15548627.2024.2374699), which is maintained by active V-
ATPase on lysosomal membrane. The authors should discuss whether Rab2, in addition
to Rab14, plays any role in lysosomal acidification in their experimental system.

recruiting the HOPS complex to promote autophagosome-lysosome fusion (PMID:
38953305). Notably, this fusion step is independent of V-ATPase-mediated
lysosomal acidification (PMID: 25959678; PMID: 26156798); thus, the role of
Rab2 and Rab14 in fusion does not imply a function in modulating lysosomal pH.
In our experimental system, lysosomal pH analysis was conducted in macrophages
with Rab gene knockdown, the data showed that unlike Rab14 knockdown, Rab2a
knockdown minimally altered lysosomal pH (Fig. 1a). Thus, Rab14 exerts a
specific function in promoting lysosomal acidification, which is not shared by
Rab2 (lines 102–105).
3. On page 7/79, lines 152-156, the authors state that while V0a1 strongly colocalized
with LAMP1-positive lysosomes in Rab14+/+ cells, it primarily colocalized with the
ER-marker, calnexin in Rab14-/- cells. The anterograde movement (from ER to Golgi)
of proteins is mediated by COPII vesicles. In addition, all COPII proteins, except Sec13,
have been reported to undergo S-palmitoylation (:10.1016/j.nbd.2025.106890), a
reversable post-translational modification of proteins by saturated fatty acids (generally
palmitate). Moreover, dynamic S-palmitoylation (palmitoylation-depalmitoylation) has
been shown to facilitate the trafficking of V0a1 to the late endosome / lysosome
(https://doi:10.1038/ncomms14612). Thus, both S-palmitoylation and depalmitoylation,
catalyzed by ZDHHC palmitoyl acyl transferases (PATs) and thioesterases, respectively,
are critical for V0a1 to successfully traffic to the late endosomal / lysosomal membrane
(https://doi:10.1098/rsob.200411). Indeed, it has been reported that the handover of
V0a1 from the sorting endosome to late endosome / lysosome requires dynamic S-
palmitoylation. Therefore, it is critically important for the authors to rule out that in
Rab14-/- cells, the dynamic S-palmitoylation of V0a1 is not compromised impairing the
assembly of VATPase multiprotein complex essential for trafficking from the ER to the
lysosomal membrane.
R: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. As advised, we performed
acyl-Rac assay to determine the S-palmitoylation of V0a1 in Rab14+/+ and Rab14-
/- cells, and we observed no significant difference in V0a1 palmitoylation levels
between Rab14+/+ and Rab14-/- cells (revised Supplementary Fig. 7b; lines 217–219,
777–792). Moreover, the S-palmitoylation of V0a1 is required for its trafficking
from the sorting endosome to the late endosomal/lysosomal membrane (PMID:
28266544), while Rab14 mainly modulates the delivery of V0a1 from the ER to
Golgi, which is a different trafficking way independent of the endosomal sorting
pathway. Taken together, Rab14 promotes V0a1 trafficking from the ER to the
lysosomal membrane independent of V0a1 S-palmitoylation.

marker, calnexin. This may suggest that the ER-Golgi trafficking is also defective in
these cells. Since COPII proteins (e.g. Sar1, Sec23/Sec24) except Sec 13 are also
reported to be S-palmitoylated (https://doi: 10.1016/j.nbd.2025.106890), and a
thioesterase (PPT1)-deficiency impairs anterograde (ER to Golgi) trafficking mediated
by COPII vesicles, it is therefore critically important for the authors to demonstrate that
dynamic S-palmitoylation of COPII-associated proteins are not adversely affected in
Rab14-/- cells.

assay to determine the S-palmitoylation of COPII-associated proteins including
Sar1, Sec23A, Sec24A, Sec24C, and Sec31A in Rab14+/+ and Rab14-/- cells, and we
observed comparable S-palmitoylation levels of these proteins in Rab14+/+ and
Rab14-/- cells (revised Supplementary Fig. 9b; lines 273–278, 777–792), indicating
that Rab14 is not involved in regulating COPII complex S-palmitoylation.
5. A role for Rab14 in stimulating the fusion of phagosomes with early endosomes but
not with late endosomes has been demonstrated in mechanistic studies
(https://doi:10.1038/sj.emboj.7601407). In case of mycobacterial pathogens, it has
been shown that Rab14 enables phagosomes to maintain early endosomal characteristics but
not those of late endosomal/lysosomal degradative components. The authors should
discuss this finding considering their proposed immune mechanism mediated by
Rab14-CAM2D-V-ATPase axis.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point. As previously explained in
our response to question #1, Rab14 has been reported to promote phagosome-early
endosome fusion while suppressing phagosome fusion with late endosomes or
lysosomes in macrophages infected with Mtb (PMID: 17082769). It should be
pointed out that Mtb is a chronic pathogen that usually hijacks host factors to
inhibit immune responses for its long-term survival (PMID: 32728204). For
example, Mtb can employ its effectors (such as PknG) to suppress Rab14-GTP
hydrolysis, leading to the constitutive activation of Rab14, which arrests
phagosomes at the early endosome stage and prevents their fusion with late
endosomes and lysosomes, thereby blocking phagosomal maturation and
pathogen clearance (PMID: 17082769; PMID: 34092182). In contrast, in
macrophages infected with heat-killed Mtb, Rab14 only transiently associates with
phagosomes, permitting their normal fusion with late endosomes and lysosomes
for bacterial clearance (PMID: 17082769). Thus, the previously observed effect of
Rab14 stimulating organellar fusion between phagosomes and early endosomes,
but not with late endosomes or lysosomes, may represent a pathogen-hijacked
state. In our study, instead of using Mtb that hijacks Rab14 function, we used
model pathogens (including Mycobacterium smegmatis, Listeria monocytogenes,
DNA virus HSV-1, and RNA virus SeV) that can be rapidly cleared by the host
immune system to investigate the uncompromised, physiological function of
Rab14, and we demonstrate that Rab14 primarily facilitates pathogen clearance
by promoting V0a1 lysosomal localization and subsequent lysosomal acidification
through suppression of CAMK2D-mediated V0a1 phosphorylation. Thus, Rab14
is a critical host restriction factor whose activity could be exploited by certain
pathogens for their immune evasion. We have expanded our discussion
accordingly (lines 433–434, 440–444, 448–451).
Minor comments:
1. Figure 1 panels g-j: The Western blot to demonstrate the processing of pro-cathepsin
D (CD) to enzymatically active-CD appears to be unclear. The pro-CD (48 kDa)
undergoes proteolytic cleavage in the lysosome by Cathepsin B and Cathepsin L,
respectively, to generate the 31kDa and 14 kDa fragments. Non-covalent dimerization
of the 31kDa and 14 kDa fragments, generates the enzymatically active-CD
(https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2008.08.099). The Western blots in Figs. 1g-1j do not
attest to this picture. It appears that the 14kDa band is missing in the blots. The use of
higher percentage gels and longer duration of electrophoresis may resolve this problem.
A similar problem is encountered in Figure 6b-e. The blots should clearly show the
presence of the 31kDa and 14kDa bands. An alternative may be to determine the CD
enzymatic activity in Rab+/+ and Rab-/- cells. The Rab14-/- cells should show
significantly reduced CD enzymatic activity compared with that in Rab14+/+ cells.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this important question and for the helpful
suggestions. In our experiments, we used two distinct antibodies targeting the
heavy chain (31 kDa) and light chain (14 kDa) of mature CTSD, respectively. Our
previous manuscript presented only the heavy chain data, in line with common
practice reported in other studies (e.g., PMID: 35287553; PMID: 31282275). In
response to the reviewer’s comment, we now provide the corresponding light chain
data derived from the same samples (revised Fig. 1e–h and Fig. 6b–e), which
similarly demonstrates that Rab14 promotes CTSD maturation. Furthermore, as
suggested by the reviewer, we additionally performed the CTSD activity assay and
confirmed that the Rab14-CAMK2D axis enhances CTSD proteolytic activity
(revised Supplementary Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 11a; lines 131–134, 364–
367, 722–728).
Reviewer #2:
The authors identified Rab14 as a restriction factor against multiple bacteria and viruses.
They showed that Rab14 binds to and inhibits CAMK2D-mediated phosphorylation of
V0a1 and thus promotes lysosome acidification for pathogen clearance. The finding of
RAB14 in V0a1 trafficking is interesting. Both imaging data and quantification analyses
need to be improved substantially to support the conclusions.
R: We thank the reviewer for these constructive comments. We have improved our
manuscript by optimizing the imaging data and adding quantification results for
the immunoblots. The following is the point-by-point response to all comments.
Major points:
1. Fluorescence images in all figures are too small to see clear subcellular localization
and the alterations under different conditions. High magnification images showing clear
subcellular compartments (ER, Golgi, lysosomes) and the localization of the target
proteins (V0a) should be provided.
R: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. We repeated the confocal
microscopy experiments with optimized conditions and provided higher
magnification and clearer images in our revised manuscript (revised Fig. 2, Fig.
3e, f, and Fig. 5i).
2. Quantification analyses are lacking in many assays.
R: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this issue. We performed quantification
analyses for the immunoblots and included these data in the revised manuscript
(revised Fig. 1e–h, Fig. 3a–d, Fig. 5a–h, Fig. 6b–e, Supplementary Fig. 4a–d, and
Supplementary Fig. 8d).
Specific comments:
1. Lysotracker staining in Fig. 1b-f should be done in cells labeled by lysosome
membrane markers such as LAMP1 or TMEM192, to confirm defects in acidification
but not number of lysosomes.
R: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. To definitively determine
whether the observed reduction in LysoTracker signal reflects impaired lysosomal
acidification rather than a decrease in lysosome number, we performed the
recommended co-staining for LAMP1 (a marker of total lysosomes) and
LysoTracker (a marker of acidified lysosomes). Our data showed that while the
LysoTracker fluorescence intensity was much higher in infected Rab14+/+
macrophages than that in infected Rab14-/- macrophages, the LAMP1 intensity
remained comparable between the two group (Fig. 1b–d; lines 112–118),
confirming that Rab14 depletion specifically compromises lysosomal acidification
without affecting lysosomal number. To further validate this finding functionally,
we performed live-cell imaging assays using the LysoSensor Yellow/Blue probe,
which mainly produces yellow fluorescence in acidic lysosomes (low pH), but blue
fluorescence in less acidic lysosomes (high pH) (PMID: 11444806). The results
consistently confirmed that Rab14 promotes lysosomal acidification
(Supplementary Fig. 3b; lines 118–124, 861–866). Together, these results from
experiments adopting two approaches conclusively demonstrate that Rab14 is
required for lysosomal acidification, independent of lysosomal biogenesis.
2. Fig. 1g-i: CTSD processing should be quantified.
Extended Fig. 2: LC3 processing should be quantified.
R: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We performed quantification
analyses for CTSD maturation (calculated by the ratio of mature CTSD heavy
chain or light chain to TUBA1A, revised Fig. 1e–h) and LC3 processing (calculated
by the LC3-II/TUBA1A ratio, revised Supplementary Fig. 4a–d). The
quantification results provide statistical validation and consistently demonstrate
that Rab14 is required for the efficient processing of both proteins.
3. Data shown in Fig. 2a-e, f are critical, but the images are unclear. High magnification
images are needed to indicate subcellular localization of V0a1 with different markers.
In Fig. 2f, lysosomal marker such as LAMP1 should be included. Lysotracker staining
shows lysosomal acidification, but it is not a suitable lysosomal marker to show V01a
trafficking to lysosomes in these experiments.
R: We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out these issues. We repeated the
confocal microscopy experiments and optimized the imaging conditions to more
clearly resolve the subcellular localization of V0a1. The double-
immunofluorescence labeling analysis of V0a1 and organelle markers revealed
strong colocalization of V0a1 with LAMP1-positive lysosomes in Rab14+/+ cells,
whereas in Rab14-/- cells, V0a1 primarily colocalized with the ER-integral protein
calnexin (revised Fig. 2a–e). Moreover, we isolated the ER and lysosomal fractions
from Rab14⁺/⁺ and Rab14⁻/⁻ cells and consistently demonstrated that Rab14
promotes the lysosomal targeting of V0a1 (revised Supplementary Fig. 5a; lines
175–179, 745–751). Furthermore, regarding lysosomal markers, as suggested by
the reviewer, we used V0a1 and the canonical lysosomal membrane protein
LAMP1 for co-immunostaining experiments, and the results showed that
pathogen infections could increase the trafficking of V0a1 to lysosomes in Rab14+/+
cells, while this effect is largely reduced in Rab14-/- cells (revised Fig. 2f). Analysis
of V0a1 levels in purified lysosomes also demonstrated a significantly higher
enrichment of V0a1 on lysosomes from Rab14+/+ cells than those from Rab14-/- cells
(revised Supplementary Fig. 6a; lines 189–191).
4. Why V0a1, but not V0a2 and a3, is affected in Rab14-deficient cells? As all of them
are expressed in macrophages, how the specific regulation of V0a1 by Rab14 is
achieved?
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this insightful question regarding the specific
regulation of V0a1, but not V0a2 or V0a3, by Rab14 in macrophages. In our
previous manuscript, we found that Rab14 selectively promotes the lysosomal
trafficking of V0a1 without affecting V0a2 or V0a3, which led us to focus on V0a1
to dissect the underlying mechanism. Mechanistical studies revealed that Rab14
binds to CAMK2D and competitively inhibits the interaction between CAMK2D
and V0a1, thus suppressing CAMK2D-mediated phosphorylation of V0a1 to
promote V0a1 binding to the COPⅡ complex for V0a1 trafficking from the ER to
Golgi and then to lysosomes. Thus, the interaction between CAMK2D and V0a1
represents the core mechanism by which Rab14 regulates V0a1 trafficking.
To further elucidate the mechanism by which Rab14 specifically regulates V0a1,
as requested by the reviewer, we detected the interaction between CAMK2D and
V0a1, V0a2, or V0a3, and we found that CAMK2D specifically bound to V0a1, but
not V0a2 or V0a3 (Supplementary Fig. 8a; lines 236–237). We further conducted
molecular docking analysis and revealed that CAMK2D bound to the Arg 179 and
Arg 198 sites of V0a1, two residues that are not conserved in V0a2 or V0a3
(Supplementary Fig. 8b, c; lines 237–239, 868–881). Consistently, the in vitro
phosphorylation assay showed that V0a1, but not V0a2 or V0a3, was
phosphorylated by CAMK2D (Supplementary Fig. 8g; lines 248–249). Taken
together, the specificity of Rab14 for V0a1 is determined by the exclusive,
structure-dependent interaction between CAMK2D and V0a1.
5. Quantification analyses should be provided in Fig. 3a-d; high magnification and more
clear images are needed in Fig. 3e, f.
R: We thank the reviewer for these helpful suggestions. We have provided
quantification results for the immunoblots in the revised Fig. 3a–d, with the
detailed methodology described in the corresponding figure legends (lines 1149–
1150, 1152–1153, 1155–1156, 1161–1162). Additionally, we repeated the confocal
microscopy experiments and provided clearer, high-magnification images in the
revised Fig. 3e–f to better illustrate the subcellular localization of V0a1.
6. Extended Fig. 5e, CAMK2D interacts with V0a1 in both Rab14+/+ and Rab14-/- cells,
which is inconsistent with the statement in the manuscript (line 209-210).
Quantification analyses should be included to support the conclusion.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. We performed quantification
analyses for the co-immunoprecipitation experiments in the previous Extended
Data Fig. 5e. The quantitative results confirmed that the interaction between
CAMK2D and V0a1 is indeed significantly stronger in Rab14-/- cells compared to
that in Rab14+/+ cells (revised Supplementary Fig. 8d), which is consistent with our
stated conclusion that Rab14 competitively inhibits the binding between
CAMK2D and V0a1.
7. The p-Ser specificity should be examined.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point regarding the p-Ser
specificity. In our experimental system for detecting the p-Ser of V0a1, we first
immunoprecipitated V0a1 followed by p-Ser immunoblotting. The critical
evidence for the specificity is that the p-Ser antibody failed to detect any signal at
the expected molecular weight when using the V0a1S19A mutant, demonstrating
that the phospho-serine signal we observed was specifically derived from V0a1 and
dependent on the S19 residue. Moreover, we generated a phosphospecific antibody
against the V0a1 S19 site. Through in vitro and in vivo phosphorylation assays
using this antibody, we confirmed that CAMK2D phosphorylates V0a1 at S19,
while Rab14 inhibits this process (Supplementary Fig. 9f, g; lines 299–303, 597–
604).
8. Where CAMK2D is localized and whether its localization is altered in Rab14-/- cells?
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this question. Through examining the
subcellular localization of CAMK2D by confocal microscopy analysis, we found
that CAMK2D exhibits a diffuse cytoplasmic distribution, and this localization
pattern remains unchanged in Rab14-/- cells (Supplementary Fig. 9a; lines 266–
270), indicating that Rab14 modulates V0a1 trafficking independent of CAMK2D
localization.
9. Quantification analyses should be provided in Fig. 5a-h, and high magnification and
more clear images are needed in Fig. 5i.
R: We thank the reviewer for these helpful suggestions. We have provided
quantification results for the immunoblots in the revised Fig. 5a–h, with the
detailed methodology described in the corresponding figure legends (lines 1205–
1206, 1212). Additionally, we repeated the confocal microscopy experiments and
provided clearer, high-magnification images in the revised Fig. 5i to better
illustrate the subcellular localization of V0a1.
10. Quantification analyses should be provided in Fig. 6b-e.
R: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We have added
quantification analyses for CTSD maturation, represented by the ratio of mature
CTSD heavy chain or light chain to TUBA1A (revised Fig. 6b–e). These
quantifications provide statistical validation and consistently demonstrate that
Rab14-CAMK2D axis is required for CTSD maturation.
Reviewer #3:
This article provides insights into how Rab14 contributes to pathogen clearance by
regulating the CAMK2D-ATPase axis. Overall, the data are informative and support
the main conclusions. I have several comments that may help strengthen the manuscript.
R: We thank the reviewer for the encouraging comments on our manuscript and
for the constructive suggestions to improve this manuscript.
1. Recent work has shown that RAB14, together with other proteins, regulates
autophagy by modulating the HOPS complex. This suggests that RAB14 may influence
autophagy independently of lysosomal acidification. In Extended Data Fig. 8, it appears
that the maturation of LC3 puncta during autophagy is entirely regulated by the Rab14-
CAMK2D axis. The authors may need to further discuss this point in the discussion. It
would be also good to explain more by new data if it’s necessary.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point. As noted by the reviewer,
a recent study in MDCK epithelial cells demonstrated that Rab14 together with
Rab2 promote autophagosome-lysosome fusion through recruiting the HOPS
complex (PMID: 38953305), indicating that Rab14 modulates autophagy
independent of the lysosomal acidification pathway that we revealed in our study.
Indeed, in our previous Extended Data Fig. 8 (revised Supplementary Fig. 12), we
monitored the dynamic autophagy flux using the mCherry-GFP-LC3 tandem
reporter. In this system, immature autophagosomes appear as yellow puncta (due
to the overlap of green and red fluorescence), whereas mature autolysosomes
display only red puncta, as the GFP signal is quenched by the acidic environment
(PMID: 38390831). Consequently, the ratio of yellow to total LC3 puncta serves as
a direct readout of autophagy flux, which is primarily dependent on lysosomal
acidification. Therefore, regardless of whether Rab14 regulates autophagosome-
lysosome fusion, its interaction with CAMK2D to control lysosomal acidification
is the key determinant of the yellow-to-total fluorescence ratio.
Moreover, to investigate whether the Rab14-CAMK2D axis regulates the
autophagosome-lysosome fusion process in our system, we examined the
colocalization of LC3 with LAMP1 in Rab14+/+, Rab14-/-, Rab14+/+Camk2d-/-, and
Rab14-/-Camk2d-/- macrophages under uninfected or infected conditions, and our
results showed that the Rab14-CAMK2D axis did not affect the fusion between
autophagosomes and lysosomes (revised Supplementary Fig. 13; lines 375–384).
Thus, Rab14-CAMK2D-mediated phosphorylation of V0a1 regulates the
localization of V0a1 on lysosomal membrane to maintain lysosomal acidification
by V-ATPase without affecting the autophagosome-lysosome fusion. It should be
noticed that our macrophage-based results are different from the previous study
reporting that Rab14 promotes autophagosome-lysosome fusion in MDCK
epithelial cells (PMID: 38953305), indicating that the function of Rab14 is cell
type-dependent, which is further supported in other studies. For instance, Rab14
promotes the trafficking of glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) from early
endosomes to the Golgi apparatus following endocytosis in adipocytes (PMID:
23444368; PMID: 26936971), while facilitating the GLUT4 translocation from the
GLUT4 storage vesicles (GSV) compartment to the plasma membrane in muscle
cells (PMID: 18701652). We have expanded our discussion accordingly (lines 444–451).
2. In Fig. 2, the conclusions rely mainly on imaging analysis. It would be valuable to
include complementary approaches to support the findings. In addition, some of the
representative images do not adequately reflect the statistical analysis. Selecting clearer
images would strengthen the presentation. Furthermore, about 50 cells were analyzed
per biological replicate. Plotting the ratios from each individual cell would make the
data more convincing.
R: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions. To further validate
the subcellular localization of V0a1 observed by imaging in the previous Fig. 2, we
performed complementary subcellular fractionation assays to assess V0a1 levels.
Specifically, to test the conclusion from the previous Fig. 2a–e that V0a1 localizes
to lysosomes in Rab14⁺/⁺ cells but to the ER in Rab14⁻/⁻ cells, we isolated ER and
lysosomal fractions and confirmed that V0a1 is predominantly enriched in
lysosomes in Rab14⁺/⁺ cells, while it is largely retained in the ER in Rab14⁻/⁻ cells
(revised Supplementary Fig. 5a; lines 175–179, 745–751). Furthermore, regarding
the finding in the previous Fig. 2i that pathogen infection increases V0a1
trafficking to lysosomes in Rab14⁺/⁺, but not Rab14⁻/⁻ cells, we purified lysosomes
from infected cells and confirmed a significantly greater enrichment of V0a1 on
lysosomes from Rab14⁺/⁺ cells compared to those from Rab14⁻/⁻ cells (revised
Supplementary Fig. 6a; lines 189–191). Additionally, we optimized our confocal
microscopy experiments and provided clearer representative images that better
align with the quantitative data (revised Fig. 2). Finally, for quantification analysis,
we have plotted the values from each of the approximately 50 individual cells
analyzed per replicate (revised Fig. 2).
3. For Fig. 3e, f, the same concern applies: some of the representative images are not
optimal and could be replaced with more suitable ones to better reflect the quantitative
analysis.
R: We thank the reviewer for raising this concern. We repeated and optimized the
confocal microscopy experiments in the previous Fig. 3e, f, and provided clearer
and more representative images that better reflect the quantitative analysis
(revised Fig. 3e, f).
4. In Fig. 5i, the authors conclude that “Rab14 promotes the trafficking of V0a1 to
lysosomes in a manner dependent on CAMK2D during pathogen infections.” However,
the data indicate that Rab14 also promotes V0a1 trafficking to lysosomes under non-
infection conditions. The conclusion should therefore be revised accordingly.
R: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. As noted by the reviewer,
Rab14 indeed promotes V0a1 trafficking to lysosomes under non-infection
conditions, as cells require a baseline level of lysosomal acidification to complete
the cellular degradation and recycling system under steady state (PMID:
37543564). We have accordingly revised the conclusion of Fig. 5i in the manuscript
(lines 344–349).
5. LysoTracker (Invitrogen, L7528) is not a direct probe for intracellular pH. To validate
the key findings, the authors are encouraged to repeat some key experiments using
LysoSensor probes, which are specifically designed for pH measurement.
R: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. As advised, we performed
live-cell imaging assays using the LysoSensor Yellow/Blue probe, which mainly
produces yellow fluorescence in acidic lysosomes (low pH), but blue fluorescence
in less acidic lysosomes (high pH) (PMID: 11444806). The results demonstrated
that compared with Rab14-/- macrophages, Rab14+/+ macrophages exhibited
stronger yellow fluorescence but weaker blue fluorescence (revised Supplementary
Fig. 3b; lines 118–124, 861–866), confirming the conclusion that Rab14 is required
for lysosomal acidification.
Minor points:
1. Line 94: The reference to “Supplementary Fig. 1” may need to be deleted.
R: As suggested by the reviewer, the reference to “Supplementary Fig. 1” has been
deleted in the revised manuscript (line 97).
2. Extended Data Fig. 2b: It would improve clarity if the long-term and short-term LC3
imaging results were presented together.
R: We thank the reviewer for this helpful suggestion. We repeated the experiments
in the previous Extended Data Fig. 2b–e, and provided the LC3 immunoblotting
results with both long-term and short-term exposures (revised Supplementary Fig.
4a–d), consistently demonstrating that Rab14 promotes autophagy flux during
multiple pathogen infections.
Once again, we greatly appreciate the reviewers for having helped us improve
this manuscript tremendously.
